newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Inventory sell-off weighs on memory chip prices.
newsitem.headline: Inventory sell-off weighs on memory chip prices.

text.p: An inventory sell-off by U.S. and Japanese chipmakers has dragged down prices for 16-megabit dynamic random access memory (DRAM) chips to around $8 and analysts on Thursday predicted further declines.
Analysts said the chips, used in everything from personal computers to calculators, hit a recent high of $10.30 in world markets in early March but have tumbled in the past few days.

Suh Sung-won, an electronics analyst with Deutsche Morgan Grenfell Capital Markets Ltd, said efforts by U.S. chipmakers and second-tier Japanese manufacturers to reduce stockpiles were behind the collapse.

He said U.S. manufacturers had taken advantage of the recent rebound in prices to clear warehouses while Japanese chipmakers were offloading stockpiles ahead of the "Golden Week" holiday at the end of this month.
"This is a return to a more fundamentally supportive level," said Matt Cleary, an analyst at HG Asia. "I think what we have seen in the last month and a half was a little bit artificial."

World prices for 16-megabit DRAM chips plunged last year from more than $50 apiece in 1995 due to excess production. In response, South Korean chipmakers agreed early last year to cut back on output to help shore up prices.
Jon Chong-hwa, analyst at Hanuri Salomon Securities, said recent price gains resulted from the production cuts.

Reflecting concerns over the industry's prospects, Standard & Poor's Corp rating agency said on Thursday it had cut the long-term outlook of South Korea's largest chipmaker Samsung Electronics Co Ltd's to negative from stable.
Samsung's share price closed unchanged on Thursday at 59,600 won ($66).

F.P. Wong, a senior manager at Taiwan's Vtech Computer, said pressure on chip prices was also coming from expectations of an imminent announcement by U.S. semiconductor giant Intel Corp about a major price reduction for central processing units (CPUs).
"Intel will have a new pricing for its CPUs in late April or early May and the price will be much lower," he said.
An official at South Korea's Hyundai Electronics, South Korea's second-largest chipmaker after Samsung, described the latest price downturn as a "temporary phenomenon".
"After the holiday, the price will rebound," he said.
But several industry analysts forecast prices would fall further to around $7 by the end of this year.
"I'm concerned about what will happen after June when Taiwanese chipmakers began producing the 16-megabit DRAM," said Bahn Young-one, an analyst at Ssangyong Securities.
"I also question how long collaboration among chipmakers to freeze production will continue," he said.
Yook Dong-jo, an analyst at C.S. First Boston, predicted prices would stay around the current $8 level as manufacturers transferred production from 16-megabit DRAMs to more powerful 64-megabit DRAMs.
Semiconductors are South Korea's largest single export item. The plunge in prices has helped swell a trade deficit and curb economic growth.

"The latest price fall will not be a further blow to the economy as the earlier market consensus for prices was $6-$7 for the second half," said Rhee Namuh, head of research at Dongbang Peregrine Securities.
Standard & Poors said its Samsung downgrade reflected concerns that the industry slump would force the company to rely on debt to finance rapid expansion.
(Conversion: $1 = 893 won)
